---
id: 'auth-third-party-custom-oidc'
title: 'Custom OIDC provider'
subtitle: 'Use any OIDC-compliant identity provider with your Supabase project'
---

Any identity provider that supports OpenID Connect (OIDC) can be used as a third-party authentication provider alongside Supabase Auth, or standalone, with your Supabase project. Use this guide for a provider that is not in the list of [supported providers](/docs/guides/auth/third-party/overview).

## Getting started

1. Check that your provider meets the [requirements](#requirements).
2. Add a Third-Party Auth integration with your provider's issuer URL in the [Dashboard](#add-the-integration-in-the-dashboard) or with the [Management API](#add-the-integration-with-the-management-api).
3. Add the `role` claim to the JWTs your provider issues.
4. Set up the Supabase client in your application.

## Requirements

Your provider must meet the [limitations](/docs/guides/auth/third-party/overview#limitations) of third-party auth:

1. It exposes an OIDC Issuer Discovery URL, served at `<issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration`.
2. It signs JWTs with an asymmetric key and includes a `kid` header parameter. Symmetrically signed JWTs, such as HS256, are not supported.
3. Its JWTs contain a `role` claim. See [Assign the role claim](#assign-the-role-claim).

The issuer URL must use HTTPS. Your project reads the signing keys from the `jwks_uri` listed in the discovery document.

## Add the integration in the Dashboard

1. In the Dashboard, go to **Authentication** > **Sign In / Providers** > [**Third-Party Auth**](/dashboard/project/_/auth/third-party).
2. Click **Add provider** and select **Custom OIDC**.
3. Enter your provider's issuer URL in **Issuer URL**, for example `https://login.example.com`.
4. Click **Add provider**.

The provider appears in the Third-Party Auth list with its issuer URL. To remove it, delete it from the same list.

## Add the integration with the Management API

Create a [personal access token](/docs/guides/platform/personal-access-tokens), then call the [create third-party auth integration](/docs/reference/api/v1-create-project-tpa-integration) endpoint with your provider's issuer URL in the `oidc_issuer_url` field. To list or remove integrations, use the [list](/docs/reference/api/v1-list-project-tpa-integrations) and [delete](/docs/reference/api/v1-delete-project-tpa-integration) endpoints.

## Supabase CLI

Custom OIDC providers are not available in the Supabase CLI. There is no `supabase/config.toml` option for them.

## Assign the role claim

Your Supabase project inspects the `role` claim in every JWT sent to it, to assign the correct Postgres role when using the Data API, Storage or Realtime authorization. Without a `role` claim, requests run as the `anon` role.

Set `role` to `authenticated` for signed-in users. Use your provider's custom claims or token template feature to add it. See your provider's documentation for the steps.

## Set up the Supabase client library

Pass an `accessToken` async function that returns your provider's JWT for the current user, or `null` if there is no signed-in user:

```typescript
import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js'

const supabase = createClient(
  'https://<supabase-project>.supabase.co',
  'SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY',
  {
    accessToken: async () => {
      return getAccessTokenFromYourProvider()
    },
  }
)
```

Replace `getAccessTokenFromYourProvider` with the call your provider's SDK offers to get the current user's JWT.

## Using RLS policies

After the client sends your provider's JWT, use RLS policies to secure access to your project's database, Storage objects and Realtime channels.

### Identify the user

The `sub` claim identifies the user. `auth.uid()` casts `sub` to `uuid`, so it fails if your provider issues subjects that are not UUIDs. Read the claim directly instead:

```sql
create policy "Users can read their own rows"
  on table_name
  for select
  to authenticated
  using (user_id = (select auth.jwt()->>'sub'));
```

Here `user_id` must be a `text` column.

### Restrict access by issuer

Your project trusts every issuer you add, and `sub` values from different issuers can collide. If you use more than one issuer, or you also use Supabase Auth, add a restrictive policy that checks the `iss` claim. For a CI/CD workflow identity issuer, such as GitHub Actions, an `iss` check is not enough. See [CI/CD workflow identity issuers](#cicd-workflow-identity-issuers).

```sql
create policy "Restrict access to trusted issuers"
  on table_name
  as restrictive
  to authenticated
  using (
    (auth.jwt()->>'iss' = 'https://<project-ref>.supabase.co/auth/v1')
    or
    (auth.jwt()->>'iss' = 'https://login.example.com')
  );
```

<Admonition type="danger">

Postgres has two types of policies: permissive and restrictive. This example uses a restrictive policy, so make sure you don't omit the `as restrictive` clause.

</Admonition>

For more on restrictive policies and on sharing the check across tables, Storage and Realtime, see the [Firebase Auth guide](/docs/guides/auth/third-party/firebase-auth#adding-an-extra-layer-of-security-to-your-projects-rls-policies-self-hosting-only).

### CI/CD workflow identity issuers

Third-party auth is for signing in your end users. CI/CD services also run OIDC issuers, but their tokens identify a workflow or a machine, not a person. Don't add these issuers as a third-party auth provider. To let a pipeline reach your project, keep a [secret API key](/docs/guides/getting-started/api-keys) in your pipeline's secrets instead. Secret keys bypass RLS, so store them with care.

<Admonition type="danger" title="CI/CD tokens are not scoped to your project">

Some of these issuers sign tokens for every account on the service, so a token from any other organization's pipeline passes your project's signature and issuer checks. Whatever Postgres role your project assigns to these tokens, any account on the service can get it, unless your RLS policies also check a claim that identifies your organization or repository. An `iss` check alone does not do this.

</Admonition>

These services run workload identity issuers:

| Service                           | Issuer URL                                                                            | Scope of the issuer         |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| GitHub Actions                    | `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`                                         | Shared by all accounts      |
| GitHub Actions, enterprise        | `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com/<enterprise-slug>`                       | One per enterprise          |
| GitHub Enterprise Cloud (GHE.com) | `https://token.actions.<subdomain>.ghe.com`, or with `/<enterprise-slug>`             | One per tenant              |
| GitHub Enterprise Server          | `https://<host>/_services/token`                                                      | One per server              |
| GitLab.com                        | `https://gitlab.com`                                                                  | Shared by all accounts      |
| CircleCI                          | `https://oidc.circleci.com/org/<organization-id>`, or `https://oidc.circleci.com`     | One per organization        |
| Bitbucket Pipelines               | `https://api.bitbucket.org/2.0/workspaces/<workspace>/pipelines-config/identity/oidc` | One per workspace           |
| Buildkite                         | `https://agent.buildkite.com`                                                         | Shared by all organizations |
| HCP Terraform                     | `https://app.terraform.io`                                                            | Shared by all organizations |
| Semaphore                         | `https://<organization>.semaphoreci.com`                                              | One per organization        |

Azure DevOps, Bitrise, Codefresh, Harness, and Spacelift also issue workload tokens. Check your service's documentation for its issuer URL and for the claims it signs.

To keep other accounts out when you do use one of these issuers, require a claim that only your pipelines carry. For GitHub Actions, `repository` holds the owner and repository name, and `repository_owner` holds the owner. Their numeric counterparts, `repository_id` and `repository_owner_id`, don't change when you rename or transfer a repository, so prefer them when you can.

This restrictive policy lets Supabase Auth users through, and accepts GitHub Actions tokens only from one repository:

```sql
create policy "Restrict GitHub Actions to one repository"
  on table_name
  as restrictive
  to authenticated
  using (
    (select auth.jwt()->>'iss') = 'https://<project-ref>.supabase.co/auth/v1'
    or (
      (select auth.jwt()->>'iss') = 'https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com'
      and (select auth.jwt()->>'repository_id') = '123456789'
    )
  );
```

Replace `123456789` with your repository's ID. To check by name instead, compare `repository` to `my-org/my-repo`.

You can also check the `sub` claim, which GitHub builds from the repository and the workflow context. A default `sub` looks like `repo:my-org/my-repo:ref:refs/heads/main`, or `repo:my-org/my-repo:environment:production` for a job that uses an environment. Use `starts_with((select auth.jwt()->>'sub'), 'repo:my-org/my-repo:')` to match every job in one repository, or match the full value to limit access to one branch or environment. Repositories created after July 15, 2026 use a `sub` that includes IDs, such as `repo:my-org@123456/my-repo@456789:ref:refs/heads/main`. Check a token from your own workflow before you write the pattern. See GitHub's [OIDC reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/oidc) for the claim list.

Other services work the same way. GitLab.com tokens carry `namespace_path`, `project_path`, `namespace_id`, and `project_id`. Check your service's documentation for the claims it signs, and use stable IDs where it offers them.

When you enter one of these issuer URLs in the Dashboard, a warning appears in the **Add custom OIDC provider** dialog. The warning doesn't block you from adding the provider. After you add one, the Security Advisor flags it with the `auth_third_party_shared_ci_issuer` check.
